---
title: "Codons"
engine: markdown
---

Every living thing runs on an information system linking DNA to proteins.
The flow of genetic information in a cell runs one way:

$$\text{DNA} \;\xrightarrow{\ \text{transcription}\ }\; \text{RNA}
\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{translation}\ }\; \text{protein}$$

This is the **central dogma of molecular biology** (Crick, 1958). A gene
is a stretch of DNA written in a four-letter alphabet of bases: A, C, G
and T. **Transcription** copies that stretch into messenger RNA, the same
message with the base U standing in for T. **Translation** then reads the
RNA message and assembles a protein from it, one amino acid at a time.

## Amino acids

Proteins are chains built from **amino acids**: small molecules with a
common backbone and one of 20 different side chains. (You may also see
the count 22: two rare extras, selenocysteine and pyrrolysine, are
installed by recoding a stop codon rather than by codons of their own,
so they sit outside the standard table below. Pyrrolysine occurs only in
some archaea and bacteria.) The side chains
range from tiny (glycine) to bulky and ring-shaped (tryptophan), from
water-repelling to charged. The sequence of amino acids determines how
the chain folds, and the fold determines what the protein does. A protein
is typically hundreds of amino acids long, so the 20-letter alphabet
supports an astronomical space of possible sequences.

The three-letter abbreviations in the table below (Phe, Leu, Ser, ...)
are the standard shorthand for the 20 amino acids.

## The genetic code

Translation reads RNA three bases at a time. Each triplet is a **codon**,
and each codon means one amino acid, or "stop". With four bases there are
$4^3 = 64$ possible codons for only 20 amino acids plus a stop signal, so
the code is **redundant**: most amino acids are spelled by more than one
codon. Leucine, serine and arginine have six spellings each; tryptophan
and methionine have exactly one. AUG doubles as the **start** signal that
begins every protein, and UAA, UAG and UGA are the three **stop** codons
that end one.

![The standard genetic code: 64 codons mapped to 20 amino acids, one
start and three stops. (OpenStax Biology 2e, CC BY 4.0)](../images/codon-table.png){width=85%}

Read it like a coordinate lookup: first base picks the row, second base
picks the column, third base picks the line within the cell. The
redundancy is not scattered at random. It is concentrated in the third
position, where a mutation often changes nothing at all. Notice that the
table's layout choice makes that pattern visible: whole cells of four
codons collapsing to a single amino acid.
